title: OET Listening Practice Test 1
instructions: OET Listening has three parts. Part A: Consultation Extracts (note-taking style). Part B: Short Workplace Extracts (main point identification). Part C: Presentation Extracts (detailed comprehension). Listen carefully and choose the best answer.

parts.title: Part A — Consultation Extracts
parts.description: Doctor-patient consultations. Listen and take notes to answer questions about specific information.

parts.title: Part B — Short Workplace Extracts
parts.description: Workplace briefings, handovers, phone calls. Identify the main point or purpose.

parts.title: Part C — Presentation Extracts
parts.description: Healthcare presentations or talks. Comprehend main ideas and supporting details.

listeningScripts.title: GP Consultation - Hypertension
listeningScripts.text:
Doctor: Good morning, Mrs Chen. I see from your notes that your last blood pressure reading was quite elevated. How have you been feeling? Patient: Well, I've noticed some headaches in the mornings, and I feel quite tired most of the time. My husband says I've been irritable too. Doctor: I see. Have you been stressed recently? Patient: Yes, my daughter's wedding is coming up in three weeks, and we're in the middle of renovating the kitchen. I'm sleeping badly. Doctor: Right. Let's check your blood pressure now. I'll also want to do some blood tests to rule out any other causes. The reading today is 158 over 98, which is higher than last time. I'm recommending we start a low-dose antihypertensive medication. I'd also like you to reduce salt in your diet, exercise regularly—at least 30 minutes daily—and try stress management techniques. Come back in two weeks so we can recheck. Patient: What about side effects? Doctor: Most people tolerate these well, but some report fatigue or dizziness initially. If you experience these, call us straightaway. Also, continue monitoring at home if you have a device. Patient: OK, I'll do that. Doctor: Before you leave, the nurse will give you information on blood pressure management. We'll also arrange those blood tests.

Doctor: Hello Tommy, let me have a look at your ears. Can you sit still for me? I'm going to use this little torch. Patient's mother: He's been pulling at his ears constantly, and he's had a fever for two days. The fever came down a bit with paracetamol. Doctor: I can see there's redness in the left ear canal. Tommy, does it hurt when I press here? Patient: Yes, it hurts. Doctor: He has acute otitis media. The eardrum looks inflamed. Has he had ear infections before? Mother: No, never. This is the first time. Doctor: OK. I'll prescribe amoxicillin for seven days. Two tablets three times daily, taken with or without food. Watch for any rash—if he develops one, stop immediately and contact us. The pain should improve within 24 to 48 hours. Use paracetamol for pain relief if needed. Avoid water in the ear while bathing. Bring him back if symptoms worsen or don't improve after five days. Any questions? Mother: How do these ear infections happen? Doctor: Usually viral infections lead to fluid accumulation behind the eardrum. In Tommy's case, bacteria have infected the fluid. It's common in young children.

Pharmacist: Good afternoon, Mr Patel. I've reviewed your medications with your GP. You're on quite a few tablets. Let me run through them. You're taking lisinopril 10 milligrams daily for blood pressure, correct? Patient: Yes, that's right. Pharmacist: And aspirin 75 milligrams daily for heart protection. Simvastatin 20 milligrams at night for cholesterol. And metformin 500 milligrams twice daily for your diabetes. Patient: That sounds right. Is that too many? Pharmacist: No, this is a reasonable combination for someone with your conditions. However, I want to check: are you taking them at the same time? Patient: Yes, all in the morning with breakfast. Pharmacist: Actually, it's better to take the simvastatin in the evening with food. And the metformin—if you're having any stomach upset, we could try the extended-release version. Patient: I have been getting a bit of stomach discomfort. Pharmacist: Let me speak with your GP about switching to extended-release metformin. In the meantime, make sure you take simvastatin at night. Also, I need to ask: are you taking any other supplements or over-the-counter medicines? Patient: Just some vitamin D. Pharmacist: That's fine with these medications. Come back in four weeks so we can check how you're getting on.

listeningScripts.title: Handover - Ward Round Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Charge Nurse: Right team, let's do the morning handover. Starting with Bay 3—that's Mrs Williams, 76, post-op day two after hip replacement. Vitals are stable, pain controlled on current analgesia. The physio will see her this afternoon for mobilisation. Drain is producing less fluid, which is good. We need to monitor the surgical wound for any signs of infection. Next is Bay 5, Mr Kumar, 82, admitted with pneumonia. His oxygen saturation improved overnight; he's now on 3 litres via nasal cannula instead of 5. Antibiotics are working well. We're planning to review his respiratory status this afternoon and might reduce oxygen further if he remains stable. Bay 7 is new—admitted last night, Miss Anderson, 34, with severe migraine and photophobia. She's on strong analgesia and antiemetic. She needs a quiet environment. Keep lighting low and reduce noise. If headache persists beyond today, neurology will assess tomorrow. Any questions before we start the round?

Nurse: Hi, this is Sarah from the community nursing team. I'm calling about a patient, Mr Roberts, who was just discharged from hospital yesterday. He has a prescription for cephalexin 500 milligrams four times daily for a leg wound infection. He asked me if he should refrigerate the suspension, and I wasn't certain. Can you advise? Pharmacist: Hi Sarah. Which suspension? Is it the oral liquid? Nurse: Yes, that's the one. Pharmacist: OK, cephalexin suspension should be stored at room temperature, not refrigerated. But it's important that after dispensing, it's only good for 14 days. The patient should shake it well before each dose. They're on it for two weeks? Nurse: That's correct—two weeks. So room temperature, shake before use, and 14-day limit. Pharmacist: Exactly. Also, if he experiences diarrhoea or any allergic reaction, he should contact his GP immediately. And remind him to complete the full course even if the wound looks better after a few days. Nurse: Will do. Thanks for confirming. Pharmacist: No problem, Sarah. Anything else? Nurse: No, that's all I needed. Cheers. Pharmacist: Bye.

listeningScripts.title: Presentation - Hand Hygiene in Healthcare
listeningScripts.text: Speaker: Today we're discussing hand hygiene, which is the single most important practice to prevent healthcare-associated infections. Despite decades of research and campaigns, compliance rates remain disappointingly low—often between 40 and 60 percent—especially among physicians. Why is this? First, healthcare environments are busy and chaotic. Secondly, many staff perceive hand hygiene protocols as bureaucratic and time-consuming. Thirdly, there's a lack of awareness about the serious consequences of lapses. The World Health Organization estimates that healthcare-associated infections affect hundreds of millions of people globally each year. In high-income countries alone, they account for substantial morbidity and mortality. So what works? Evidence shows that multifaceted programmes are most effective. These include: provision of accessible alcohol-based hand sanitizers at each patient's bed; mandatory training for all staff; visual reminders such as posters; feedback on compliance rates to departments; and leadership engagement. Institutions that implemented these strategies saw compliance increase from 50 percent to over 85 percent within one year. The most successful programmes also involved reducing unnecessary antibiotic use, as antibiotic resistance is closely linked to infection control. In conclusion, hand hygiene is not just an individual responsibility—it's a system-wide commitment that requires everyone, from nurses to administrators, to prioritise patient safety.
